Wie man eine Tasse Kaffee trägt

The driving exam was scheduled for Thursday, the twenty-eighth of August, at eight in the morning, on the M10 line, from Hauptbahnhof to Warschauer Straße and back, once right across the city. Leo had driven the route so many times in recent weeks, with Herr Schäfer beside him, that, as he had told Abena, “he could have driven it in his sleep, if that weren't expressly forbidden”. He knew every stop, every set of points, every traffic light that stayed red too long and every spot where tourists with wheelie cases crossed the tracks without looking. Even so, he slept only three hours the night before. Ludwig and Hotte had just come back from Sibiu, on Wednesday evening, after twenty-six hours on the train, and Ludwig slept even less than Leo, as Lena found when she saw a light in his kitchen at five in the morning.

At half past six, Ludwig knocked on the living-room door, behind which Leo, as before every important day since March, had slept on the sofa. He stood there in his dressing gown, with a thermos of coffee and a cup, an old white china cup with the faded BVB logo, which he had had since nineteen sixty-eight. He filled it to the brim, so full that the coffee almost spilled over, and handed it to Leo. “Carry it to the kitchen table,” he said. “Without spilling a drop.” Leo looked at him, puzzled. Then he carried the cup, four metres, along the hall, slowly, and when he arrived, he hadn't spilled a drop. “See?” said Ludwig. “That's how you pull away. Not with your foot. With the cup in your head.” His own instructor had taught him that, he said, in nineteen sixty-eight, with exactly this cup, and he had kept it ever since, for exactly this morning, without knowing it would come.

Abena had already had her driving exam on Tuesday, on the M4, and had passed, of course, with feedback that, as she read it out to Leo on the phone, was “almost embarrassingly good”. Afterwards she had given him just one piece of advice: “Don't look at the clipboard. If he's writing, it doesn't mean anything. He's always writing. He even writes when there's nothing to write. I think he draws trams.” Leo had laughed. But now, on Thursday morning, with the full cup in his hand and Ludwig's eyes on his back, he thought that Abena and Ludwig had basically said the same thing, just in different words: don't look at what makes you nervous. Look at the tracks. And carry the cup.

Herr Brenner, the examiner, was waiting at Hauptbahnhof, with a clipboard and a face that gave nothing away. It was the same Herr Brenner who had examined Leo in July in the specialist interview, and he greeted him with a brief nod and the words: “Drive as if I weren't here.” That was, as Leo said later, the hardest instruction he had ever been given. Because Herr Brenner was there, and how. He sat beside him in the cab, wrote non-stop on his clipboard and didn't say a single word the whole way, except in two places where he said “Hm”, which Leo took each time as a sign of catastrophe.

The drive began calmly. Leo pulled away the way you carry a cup of coffee and stopped the way you put it down. At Nordbahnhof a man with headphones was standing much too close to the edge of the platform, with his back to the track, absorbed in his phone, and Leo saw him from a distance, slowed down, gave a short warning signal, and the man turned round in alarm and stepped back before the tram even got near him. Herr Brenner noted something. At Zionskirchplatz a dog crossed the tracks, a small white terrier without a lead, followed by a desperate owner, and Leo stopped, waited until they were both on the pavement and only then moved on. Herr Brenner said “Hm” for the first time.

At the Bernauer Straße stop an elderly lady with a walking frame got on, very slowly, step by step, and behind her a group of schoolchildren waited, looking impatiently at their phones. The timetable on Leo's screen showed one minute's delay. Then two. Leo waited. He waited until the lady was inside, until she had found a seat, until the walking frame was standing securely, and only when she had sat down and nodded to him through the glass did he close the doors and pull away. Slowly. The way you carry a cup of coffee filled to the brim. The lady felt nothing of the pulling away. She just looked out of the window. Herr Brenner noted something, more than usual. Leo would have given a lot to know what. But he didn't look. He looked at the tracks.

Then, at Warschauer Straße, at the terminus, came the moment Leo later called “the exam within the exam”. The passengers got off, Leo pressed the button to close the doors, and the rear door stayed open. It couldn't be closed. A red light was flashing on the screen. Leo felt the blood rush to his head. He didn't know whether it was a real fault or whether Herr Brenner had caused it on purpose to test him. It was, as he found out later, a real one. But that didn't matter. He did what had to be done. He informed the control centre, calmly, in clear sentences. He went to the back, tried to close the door manually, and when it couldn't be closed, he locked it out of use, put up the sign “Tür defekt” (Door out of order) and made an announcement for the new passengers who were already getting on: “Dear passengers, the rear door is unfortunately out of service. Please use the other doors. Thank you for your understanding.”

Herr Brenner said “Hm” for the second time. Then they went back, right across the city, and Leo pulled away the way you carry a cup and stopped the way you put it down, and at the Eberswalder Straße stop, in the middle of the Kastanienallee area, he saw out of the corner of his eye, in the window of the café «Bei Ingrid», which could only just be seen from the stop, a row of faces. Lena. Elif. Hotte, with his tram driver's cap. And in the middle, on a chair someone had moved to the window, Ludwig, with the old white cup in his hand. Leo didn't ring the bell. That would have been against the regulations, in the middle of an exam. But he raised, very briefly, two fingers from the controller. Ludwig raised the cup.

At Hauptbahnhof, when the tram had stopped and the last passengers had got off, Herr Brenner put down his clipboard and looked directly at Leo for the first time that morning. “So, Herr Brandt,” he said. “First: you've passed. Now the feedback, so that you know why.” And then he gave him the feedback, which Leo later wrote down word for word in his grandfather's small grey notebook, on the page after Ingrid's drawing. What had struck him positively: the forward-looking driving style, the man at Nordbahnhof, the dog at Zionskirchplatz. The composed reaction to the door fault, everything according to the regulations, and the announcement, “friendly, which isn't in the regulations but is much appreciated”. What could be improved: pulling away, at the first three stops, a little jerky. “Not after that,” said Herr Brenner. “After that you drove as if you had a cup of coffee on the controller.”

Leo thanked him. He said: “I'll take that on board,” as he had practised, and then, because he couldn't help himself any longer: “May I ask why you said «Hm» twice?” Herr Brenner looked at him, and for the first time something twitched in his face which in another man would have been a smile. “The first time,” he said, “because of the dog. Most candidates honk the dog away. You waited. The second time because of the announcement. You said «Thank you for your understanding». Hardly anyone says that any more.” He stood up, took his clipboard and shook Leo's hand. “Congratulations, Herr Brandt. You start on the first of October. Six months' probation. Then you drive on your own.”

In the evening, in the café, when the brass bell had already rung for the fifth time and Lena had stopped counting the guests coming to congratulate Leo, Leo sat with Ludwig at the table by the window. Between them stood the old white cup with the BVB logo. Ludwig pushed it across the table. “It's yours now,” he said. Leo wanted to protest, but Ludwig raised his hand. “My instructor gave it to me on the day I passed,” he said. “His name was Herr Wilke. He died in nineteen ninety. He said: if you ever teach someone how to pull away, pass it on.” Ludwig smiled. “I never taught anyone how to pull away. Until this morning.”

At that very moment Elif's phone rang. It was Frau Petersen from the care home. Grete wanted to know how the exam had gone, she said, and didn't want to hear it from Frau Petersen but from the candidate himself. Elif gave the phone to Leo. At first Leo heard only breathing, slow, heavy breathing. Then Grete's voice, very quiet but clear: “Well? Did you pass?” “I passed,” said Leo. “With a cup of coffee.” A pause. Then a sound that was a laugh. “Your grandfather got that from Herr Wilke,” Grete whispered. “And Herr Wilke got it from his wife. She worked in the cloakroom at the Konzerthaus. In nineteen fifty-six. She held my coat. Without spilling a drop.” Leo didn't quite understand what she meant, and when he wanted to ask, Grete had already hung up. Ludwig looked at him and slowly shook his head. “She knows everybody in this city,” he said. “Everybody who ever carried something without dropping it.”

Hotte, who was sitting at the next table and had of course heard everything, cleared his throat. “That ain't true,” he said. “You taught me too. In nineteen sixty-nine. I was an instructor and couldn't pull away without the passengers fallin' over. You showed me the cup. But you never gave it to me.” Ludwig looked at him. “You never said it helped,” he said. “It didn't help neither,” said Hotte. “I carried on drivin' like an ox. But I never forgot.” Everyone laughed. And Leo took the cup, held it for a moment in both hands, then stood up, went over to Hotte and set it down on the table in front of him, for a moment, very carefully, without spilling a drop, although it was empty. Then he took it back. “Now you've had it once too,” he said. Hotte said nothing. He just nodded. And for the first time anyone in the café could remember, Hotte couldn't think of a joke.

Later, when the café was empty, Leo washed the old cup himself, in the little kitchen behind the counter, with hot water and very carefully, and dried it with the blue-and-white checked tea towel that Dr Vogt had hung that evening on the hook next to the bell. Then he wrapped it in a napkin and put it in his rucksack, next to the small grey notebook. On the first of October, on his first day of service, it stood in his cab, on the shelf next to the controller, empty, just as a witness.
